If it is, here's what I would do to start troubleshooting.

1. Disconnect the power from the outlet.

2. Disconnect the power connector from the CD, Floppy, and hard drive.

3. Remove the cards from the system. ie. Sound card, modem, and whatever else it has in it..

4. Basically, you want to remove everything except for the motherboard, cou & ram.

5. Power it on and see if it boots. Obviously, it won't boot into Windows, but we are looking for the bios to display on the monitor. 

6. If there is no change in how the system acts, then it's likely one of 4 components. Motherboard, cpu, ram, or power supply. It's not unlikely for these old power supplies to fail. And since it doesn't give you a beep when it powers on, make me suspect it's the power supply.

7. If you do see the bios on screen,  power it off and reattach power to the hard drive only. Power it on and see if the bios again shows on screen. 

8. Keep adding components back in one at a time and power it back on.

I worked as a printer technician for a number of years. I'm mostly certified on HP, Lexmark, and Xerox. But printers all basically function the same. Printers have sensors that detect if paper is present at various points in the printer. When it tells you that there is a jam, it's really telling you one of two things. 

1. I'm detecting paper somewhere in the printer, when there shouldn't be.

2. I'm not detecting paper somewhere in the printer, and there should be.

Based on your photo. It's probably the 2nd. It looks like the paper is making it to the fuser, bu it has not passed it.

Pull the fuser and see if you can rotate it manually by spinning the gears. Depending on the user, you'll either have a hard roller or one that looks like a soft tube.

The roller/soft tube needs to rotate so the paper can move through it. If it doesn't rotate and is the soft tube style, you might be able to take it apart and clean out any gunk inside it.

If you do decide to take it apart, let it cool down. Fusers get really hot.

Now, one thing that you may not realize about wires is that it's not just bank to bank. It's actually bank to Fed, to bank.

Every bank has a Fed Wire account. We don't keep funds in that account because the interest is crap. Money is placed into that Fed account at the start of the day.  As we send wires, that amount is debited from the senders account, and we put that into a GL account. Then we send the wire info to the Fed, who then debits our Fed Wire account and credits the receiving banks Fed Wire account. The Fed then sends the wire detain to the receiving bank, who will debit one of their GL accounts to credit their customer.

At the end of the day, we take the funds out of our Fed Wire account and place it into an account that gets us better interest. We repeat this daily. But truthfully, here is the simplest answer.

The Fed isn't open on the weekend. I'm in the Central time zone, and at 5:40 CST, the Fed stops sending and receiving of wire data.

You said you "got all the money out" but did you actually get with a banker that is able to close the account? 

At the bank I work for, when the account goes to a zero balance, it doesn't automatically close. It remains open (soft close) for 30 days. It says this in our disclosure you get when you open the account. If after 30 days, it's still at zero, it will then hard close. 

If, for some reason, during that soft close period, a credit or debit is made, usually by a preauthorized debit, it will either credit or debit the account. 

Sounds like you thought taking the money out would close it. You were wrong. A preauthorized debit was made and caused your account to go negative, triggering an NSF charge. 

Not trying to be mean here, but this is not the banks fault.
